concepts.name: Physics and its realm
concepts.why: Physics is concerned with describing the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time, and it is especially interested in what fundamental mechanisms underlie every phenomenon. A surprisingly small and unified set of physical laws explains what we observe, and that underlying order is what makes the subject worth studying.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the passage on the realm of physics; conceptual questions 7 and 9 ask where its classical branch applies. No exercise tests the definition on its own.

concepts.name: Model
concepts.why: A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult or impossible to display directly, such as the planetary model of the atom. It is justified by experiment but accurate only under limited situations, and it lets us picture what we cannot see.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; conceptual questions 1, 2 and 6 ask what a model is, how it differs from a theory, and whether its validity can be limited.

concepts.name: Theory
concepts.why: To a scientist a theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, supported by scientific evidence and verified many times by different groups of researchers. It should describe every aspect of any system within its domain, and an experiment that contradicts it means the theory is thrown out or modified.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; conceptual questions 2, 3, 4 and 6 turn on what makes a theory valid.

concepts.name: Law
concepts.why: A law uses concise language, often a single equation such as F = ma, to describe a generalized pattern in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and repeated experiments. A law describes a single action, whereas a theory explains a whole group of related phenomena.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding asks what can be known about a new law before hearing it; conceptual question 6 compares the validity required of a law with that of a model.

concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.why: The scientific method is the process scientists follow as they inquire about the world: an observation and a question, some research, a hypothesis, an experiment to test it, and a conclusion drawn from the results. The cornerstone is observation, since science must describe the universe as it is.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the car that will not start is worked through as an example; conceptual question 5 asks how strict the criteria for believing a result must be.

concepts.name: Classical physics
concepts.why: Classical physics is the physics that developed from the Renaissance to the end of the 19th century. It is an excellent approximation when matter moves at less than about 1% of the speed of light, when objects are large enough to be seen with a microscope, and when only weak gravitational fields such as the Earth’s are involved, which is why most of this text is devoted to it.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the boxed limits on the laws of classical physics; conceptual questions 7 and 9 ask when classical physics applies, the second for a satellite at 7500 m/s.

concepts.name: Modern physics
concepts.why: Modern physics consists of two revolutionary theories, relativity and quantum mechanics, which deal with the very fast and the very small. Relativity must be used above about 1% of the speed of light or in a strong gravitational field, and quantum mechanics for objects smaller than can be seen with a microscope; their combination, relativistic quantum mechanics, is the best universally applicable theory we have.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for modern physics, relativity and quantum mechanics; conceptual question 8 asks when relativistic quantum mechanics is necessary.

concepts.name: Physical quantity
concepts.why: A physical quantity is defined either by specifying how it is measured or by stating how it is calculated from other measurements. Distance and time are defined by methods for measuring them, whereas average speed is defined as distance traveled divided by time of travel.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the section summary; Example 1.1 calculates average speed from a distance and a time.

concepts.name: Units
concepts.why: Measurements of physical quantities are expressed in terms of units, which are standardized values. Without them it would be extremely difficult to express and compare measured values in a meaningful way; the two major systems in use are SI units and English units.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for units, SI units and English units; conceptual question 1; every problem in the section converts a value from one unit to another.

concepts.name: Fundamental units
concepts.why: The most fundamental physical quantities can be defined only in terms of the procedure used to measure them, and their units are called fundamental units. In this text they are length, mass, time, and electric current, measured in the meter, the kilogram, the second, and the ampere.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for fundamental units, second, meter and kilogram; Table 1.1; Check Your Understanding 1 asks which fundamental unit describes a hummingbird’s wingbeat.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.why: All other physical quantities, such as force and electric charge, can be expressed as algebraic combinations of length, mass, time, and current; speed, for example, is length divided by time. The units of such quantities are called derived units.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding 2 asks what a cubic centimeter being a milliliter says about the SI units.

concepts.name: Metric prefixes
concepts.why: The metric system is convenient for calculation because its units are categorized by factors of 10, and a standard set of prefixes lets the same unit be used over extremely large ranges of values. Distances in meters suit construction, kilometers suit air travel, and nanometers suit optical design, with no need to invent new units.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term for the metric system; Table 1.2; Check Your Understanding 1 asks for the prefix that fits a hummingbird’s wingbeat; conceptual question 1; problems 7 and 9.

concepts.name: Order of magnitude
concepts.why: The order of magnitude of a value is the power of 10 that sets its scale. The numbers 800 and 450 can both be written as a number times 10², so they are of the same order of magnitude; the diameter of an atom is of order 10⁻¹⁰ m and the diameter of the Sun of order 10⁹ m.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Table 1.3 of known lengths, masses and times; Check Your Understanding 1 asks which factor of 10 fits a measurement; the approximation problems of section 1.4 read their inputs from Table 1.3.

concepts.name: Conversion factor
concepts.why: A conversion factor is a ratio expressing how many of one unit are equal to another unit, such as 1000 meters in 1 kilometer or 60 seconds in 1 minute. Multiplying by the factor that cancels the unwanted unit leaves the desired unit in its place.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the 80 m to 0.080 km conversion in the text; Example 1.1; problems 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.

concepts.name: Convert a value from one unit to another
concepts.why: To convert, list the units you have and the units you want, find the conversion factor between them, and multiply so that the units cancel. If the factor is written upside down the units do not cancel, so checking the units of the answer is part of the method.
concepts.evidence: Example 1.1 converts an average speed to km/h and to m/s; problems 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 are conversions.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.why: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the correct value for that measurement. Three measurements of 11.1, 11.2 and 10.9 inches of paper that is 11.0 inches long are accurate; a measurement of 12 inches is not.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the GPS bull’s-eye passage; conceptual question 1 asks how accuracy and uncertainty are related.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.why: The precision of a measurement system refers to how close the agreement is between repeated measurements made under the same conditions, that is, to the spread of the measured values. A measuring system can be accurate but not precise, or precise but not accurate.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the GPS bull’s-eye passage; the precision of a measuring tool decides how many digits a measurement can carry.

concepts.name: Uncertainty $A \pm \delta A$
concepts.why: Uncertainty is a quantitative measure of how much your measured values deviate from a standard or expected value, a disclaimer on the number: 45,000 miles plus or minus 500. All measurements contain some uncertainty, from the measuring device, the skill of the person, irregularities in the object, and anything else that affects the outcome.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the fevers-or-chills note; Check Your Understanding 1 asks whether a stopwatch can tell two sprint times apart; conceptual questions 1 and 2; problems 11, 15 and 17.

concepts.name: Percent uncertainty, $\%\,\text{unc} = \frac{\delta A}{A} \times 100\%$
concepts.why: One way to express uncertainty is as a percent of the measured value: the uncertainty divided by the value, times 100%. A bag of apples weighed at 5.1 lb with an uncertainty of 0.4 lb has a percent uncertainty of 8%.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Example 1.2; problems 1, 3, 9 and 11.

concepts.name: Method of adding percents
concepts.why: There is an uncertainty in anything calculated from measured quantities. When the measurements going in have small uncertainties, the percent uncertainty in a quantity calculated by multiplication or division is the sum of the percent uncertainties in the items used to make the calculation: a floor 4.00 m by 3.00 m, known to 2% and 1%, has an area of 12.0 m² known to 3%.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the floor-area passage; problems 11, 15 and 17 ask for the uncertainty in a rate, a volume and an area.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.why: When we express measured values we can list only as many digits as the measuring tool gave us, and the last digit written down is the first digit with some uncertainty. Counting the digits from the first measured digit on the left through the last on the right gives the number of significant figures, and zeros are significant except when they serve only as placekeepers.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the ruler and caliper passage; the rules for zeros; Check Your Understanding 2 counts the significant figures in five measurements; problems 5 and 7.

concepts.name: Significant figures in multiplication and division
concepts.why: For multiplication and division, the result should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity having the least significant figures entering into the calculation. A circle whose radius is known to two figures has an area known to two figures, even though π is good to at least eight.
concepts.evidence: The area of a circle worked in the text; Check Your Understanding 3(b); problems 5, 7 and 13.

concepts.name: Significant figures in addition and subtraction
concepts.why: For addition and subtraction, the answer can contain no more decimal places than the least precise measurement. Potatoes weighed on scales good to 0.01 kg, 0.001 kg and 0.1 kg add up to a mass that can be given only to the tenth of a kilogram.
concepts.evidence: The potatoes worked in the text; Check Your Understanding 3(a) adds three bag weights.

concepts.name: Make a reasonable approximation
concepts.why: Physicists, other scientists and engineers often need approximations or “guesstimates” for a quantity, based on formulae whose inputs are known only to limited accuracy. Scaling up from a known quantity, such as the height of a person, gives an estimate good to an order of magnitude, which is enough to rule out unrealistic numbers and to guide an approach.
concepts.evidence: Examples 1.3 and 1.4 estimate the height of a building and of a trillion dollars in bills; Check Your Understanding asks for the area of a basketball court; problems 1, 3, 5 and 7.

concepts.name: Reference frame
concepts.why: A position is always given relative to something, such as the Earth, a whiteboard, or the cabin of an airplane. Choosing the reference frame is the first step in describing any motion.
concepts.evidence: Defined in the text ("position relative to a convenient reference frame"); the AP question separates position from displacement, which only makes sense once a frame is fixed.

concepts.name: Position
concepts.why: The position of an object is where it is at a particular time, given as a coordinate with a sign on the chosen axis. Every other quantity in one-dimensional kinematics is built from positions and times.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the AP question distinguishes position from distance traveled and displacement.

concepts.name: Displacement, $\kdx = \kxf - \kxo$
concepts.why: Displacement is the change in position, that is, the final position minus the initial position. It has a sign, and the sign gives the direction. In kinematics we nearly always deal with displacement rather than with the path taken.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (a); problems 1 and 3 part (c); AP question.

concepts.name: Distance (magnitude of displacement)
concepts.why: Distance is the magnitude of the displacement, so it has no sign. It is easy to confuse with distance traveled, which is why the text treats the two separately.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (c); problems 1 and 3 part (b); conceptual question 2.

concepts.name: Distance traveled (path length)
concepts.why: Distance traveled is the total length of the path, and it can be much greater than the magnitude of the displacement. For example, a professor who paces 150 m during a lecture may end up only 2.0 m from where she started.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (b); problems 1 and 3 part (a); conceptual questions 1 to 3.

concepts.name: Constant-acceleration model
concepts.why: In this section we assume that acceleration is constant. Then the average acceleration equals the acceleration at every instant, and the average velocity is simply the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. The kinematic equations all follow from this assumption, and many real motions can be described in pieces within which it holds.
concepts.evidence: Definition in the text ("acceleration is constant"); exercises ap-marble, p6, p18 test whether the learner knows when the model applies.

concepts.name: $\kx = \kxo + \kvb\kt$
concepts.why: Displacement equals the average velocity multiplied by the elapsed time. This is the definition of average velocity rearranged, so it holds whether or not the acceleration is constant.
concepts.evidence: Tested directly by p7, p8; used in p11, p13, p14.

concepts.name: $\kvb = \tfrac{\kvo + \kv}{2}$
concepts.why: When acceleration is constant, velocity changes at a steady rate, so the average velocity is the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. This step turns the definition of average velocity into the equations for displacement.
concepts.evidence: Tested by p7, p8; required to derive x-quadratic and v-squared.

concepts.name: $\kv = \kvo + \ka\kt$
concepts.why: The final velocity depends on both the size of the acceleration and the time over which it acts. A modest acceleration that lasts a long time can produce a very large velocity.
concepts.evidence: Tested by cyu-rocket, ai-rel-1, p1 to p5; used in most later problems.

concepts.name: $\kx = \kxo + \kvo\kt + \tfrac12\ka\kt^2$
concepts.why: Under constant acceleration, the displacement grows with the square of the elapsed time. For example, a dragster starting from rest covers only one quarter of the track in the first half of its run.
concepts.evidence: Tested by ai-rel-2, ap-marble, p5, p9, p10, p17.

concepts.name: $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 + 2\ka\kdx$
concepts.why: This equation relates velocity to displacement without involving time. Because the stopping distance of a car grows with the square of its speed, halving the speed reduces the stopping distance to one quarter.
concepts.evidence: Tested by ai-rel-3, p11 to p16, p18.

concepts.name: Choose the equation from knowns and unknowns
concepts.why: To solve a problem, first list the quantities you know and the quantity you want to find, and then choose the equation in which the quantity you want is the only unknown. This is the skill that Putting Equations Together teaches and that multi-step problems test.
concepts.evidence: Taught explicitly as a problem-solving strategy; tested by p5, p7, p19, p20, p21.

concepts.name: Interpret the solution physically
concepts.why: The algebra can give two roots, a negative time, or a square root with two signs, but only one of these describes the motion. Deciding which solution is physically reasonable is part of solving the problem.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.13 rejects the negative time root; p10(b) and p17 ask the learner to judge whether a result makes sense.

concepts.name: Restoring force
concepts.why: When an object is displaced from its equilibrium position, the deformation creates a force in the opposite direction, which pushes the object back. Without such a force there is no oscillation, because the object would simply move in a straight line at constant speed.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding 1; the AP question on the meaning of the minus sign.

concepts.name: Force constant $\kk$
concepts.why: The force constant tells how stiff a system is. The larger $\kk$ is, the greater the restoring force for the same displacement, and the stiffer the system. It is the slope of the graph of restoring force against displacement, in newtons per meter.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; every problem in the section asks for the force constant; Check Your Understanding 1 asks how to make the ruler stiffer.

concepts.name: Hooke’s law, $\kF = -\kk\kx$
concepts.why: The simplest oscillations occur when the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement. This is Hooke’s law, and the minus sign says that the force points opposite to the displacement. Knowing the force and the displacement gives the force constant, which is what most problems in this section ask for.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.1; problems 1, 3 and 5; the AP question on the minus sign. The book names the law in section 5.3 for stress and strain; the node is introduced here and will be reinforced by 5.3 when that section is built.

concepts.name: Elastic potential energy, $\kPE = \tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kx^2$
concepts.why: Deforming a system takes work, and if nothing goes into heat, sound, or motion, all of that work is stored as elastic potential energy. The work is the area under the graph of applied force against deformation, a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kx^2$. When the system is released, that energy can become kinetic energy, as it does for the dart of a toy gun.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.2; Check Your Understanding 2; conceptual question 1; problem 3.

concepts.name: Periodic motion
concepts.why: A motion that repeats itself at regular time intervals, such as a plucked guitar string or a mass on a spring moving up and down, is periodic. Each repetition takes the same time as the one before it, which is what makes a period and a frequency meaningful.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding asks for an event in your life that occurs regularly.

concepts.name: Period $\kT$
concepts.why: The period is the time to complete one oscillation. Its units are usually seconds, but may be any convenient unit of time. The word applies to the time for any event, repetitive or not, but here it is the time for one cycle of a periodic motion.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; the AP item; problems 1, 2 and 3.

concepts.name: Frequency $\kf$
concepts.why: Frequency is the number of events per unit time. For periodic motion it is the number of oscillations per unit time, measured in hertz, where one hertz is one cycle per second. A count of cycles divided by the time they took gives the frequency, whether or not the count is made over one second.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; the AP item; problems 2, 4, 5 and 6.

concepts.name: Period and frequency, $\kf = 1/\kT$
concepts.why: If one cycle takes a time $\kT$, then $1/\kT$ cycles fit into each unit of time, so the frequency is the reciprocal of the period and the period is the reciprocal of the frequency. Given either one, the other follows at once.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.3; the AP item; problems 1 to 4.

concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.why: When the net force on a system can be described by Hooke’s law and there is no damping, the system oscillates with equal displacement on either side of equilibrium. This is simple harmonic motion, the simplest and most common kind of oscillation, and the system is a simple harmonic oscillator.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms simple harmonic motion and simple harmonic oscillator; conceptual questions 1 and 3; Check Your Understanding 1.

concepts.name: Amplitude $\kX$
concepts.why: The amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. It has the units of the displacement, meters for an object on a spring, and it is related to the energy in the oscillation. In one full period the object covers four amplitudes of ground.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding 1 and 2; the AP item on the distance covered in one period, placed here from 16.1.

concepts.name: Period of a simple harmonic oscillator, $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$
concepts.why: The period and frequency of a simple harmonic oscillator depend on the mass and the force constant alone, not on the amplitude. A stiffer system has a shorter period and a more massive one a longer period. Because the period is constant, a simple harmonic oscillator can be used as a clock.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.4; AP question 2; problems 1, 3, 6 and 9; conceptual questions 2, 4, 5 and 6; Check Your Understanding 1 for the independence of amplitude.

concepts.name: Position, velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion
concepts.why: The displacement in any simple harmonic motion is a cosine of time, $\kx(t) = \kX\cos(2\pi\kt/\kT)$. The velocity is a sine with maximum $\kvmax = 2\pi\kX/\kT = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$, zero at the turning points and greatest through equilibrium, and the acceleration is a cosine opposite in direction to the displacement. These are the sine waves that link simple harmonic motion to waves.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding 2; the graphs of Figure 16.12.

concepts.name: Simple pendulum
concepts.why: A simple pendulum is a small mass, the bob, hung from a light string. Displaced along its arc, it feels a net force of $-m\kg\sin\theta$ back toward the lowest point, because the tension cancels the part of the weight along the string. For small displacements it is a simple harmonic oscillator.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; AP question 3.

concepts.name: Restoring force on a pendulum, $\kF \approx -\frac{m\kg}{L}\ks$
concepts.why: For angles below about 15°, $\sin\theta$ and $\theta$ differ by 1% or less, so the restoring force $-m\kg\sin\theta$ becomes $-m\kg\theta$, and with $\ks = L\theta$ it is $-\frac{m\kg}{L}\ks$. That is Hooke’s law with a force constant $\kk = m\kg/L$, which is what makes the pendulum a simple harmonic oscillator.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (a 12° swing is within the small-angle range); the derivation that Example 16.5 rests on.

concepts.name: Period of a simple pendulum, $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{L/\kg}$
concepts.why: Putting $\kk = m\kg/L$ into $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$ cancels the mass and leaves $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{L/\kg}$. Only the length and the acceleration due to gravity affect the period; the mass does not, and the amplitude hardly does for small swings. This is why a pendulum keeps time.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.5; AP questions 2 and 3; conceptual question 1; every problem in the section.

concepts.name: Measuring $\kg$ with a pendulum
concepts.why: Squaring the period formula and solving for $\kg$ gives $\kg = 4\pi^2 L/\kT^2$. If the length is known precisely and the period is timed over many swings at a small angle, this gives the local acceleration due to gravity to several digits, which matters in geological exploration.
concepts.evidence: The section’s learning objective; Example 16.5; AP question 2; the Take-Home Experiment; problems 7 and 13.

concepts.name: Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator, $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kx^2 = \text{constant}$
concepts.why: A simple harmonic oscillator has no dissipative forces, so its energy is shared between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy with the total constant. The energy goes completely from one form to the other as the system oscillates: all potential at the turning points, all kinetic through equilibrium. Started from rest at $\kx = \kX$, the total is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$.
concepts.evidence: The AP item on the internal energy of a 1 kg oscillator; AP question 4 of section 16.3 (the energy at the centre), placed here; conceptual question 1; problem 2(b); problem 1(b), with gravity.

concepts.name: Speed in simple harmonic motion, $\kv = \pm\kvmax\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2}$
concepts.why: Solving the conservation of energy for the velocity gives the speed at every position, greatest at equilibrium and zero at the turning points, with $\kvmax = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$. The maximum velocity is proportional to the amplitude, greater for stiffer systems, and smaller for larger masses.
concepts.evidence: The section’s learning objective; Example 16.6; Check Your Understanding 1 and 2; problem 1(a) through the frequency.

concepts.name: The projection of uniform circular motion is simple harmonic motion
concepts.why: A point moving round a circle at constant angular velocity $\kw$ has a projection on a fixed axis at $\kx = \kX\cos\kw\kt$, and with $\kw = 2\pi/\kT$ this is exactly the position of a simple harmonic oscillator. The shadow of a ball on a turntable therefore moves in simple harmonic motion, and the speed and the period of any simple harmonic oscillator can be read off the circle: the similar triangles give $\kv = \kvmax\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2}$, and one revolution gives $\kT = 2\pi\kX/\kvmax = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding; the section summary. The AP item on the range of $x = A\sin\omega t$ is unkeyed and left out.
